# Runledger LLM Integration Summary

Runledger is a Rust workspace for durable jobs, workflow orchestration, and
worker runtime loops on PostgreSQL. This summary describes release 0.11.0,
including the 0.6 through 0.11 continuation, recovery, replay, metrics, event,
coordination, lease-identity, and durable enqueue-intent contracts. The minimum
supported versions are Rust 1.88 and PostgreSQL 18.

This file is for downstream agents integrating Runledger into another
application. It is not an AGENTS.md file and should not be treated as maintainer
instructions for this repository.

## Imports

```rust
use runledger_core::prelude::*;
use runledger_postgres::prelude::*;
use runledger_runtime::prelude::*;
```

The preludes intentionally avoid generic `Result` and `Error` aliases so they
can be imported together.

## Choose The API

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| One independent retried unit of work | `enqueue_job` with `JobEnqueue` |
| Commit application state and future work before its definition exists | `JobEnqueueIntent` + `record_job_enqueue_intent_tx` |
| Multi-step work with dependencies | `WorkflowDagBuilder` (simple) or workflow run/step builders (advanced) |
| Multi-step work with a durable JSON result | Declare a result step and use workflow handle APIs |
| Fan-out, fan-in, or ordered stages | `WorkflowDagBuilder::after_success` / `after_terminal` |
| Human/API approval or another external gate | External workflow steps |
| Delayed or recurring entrypoint | `upsert_job_schedule` with `JobScheduleUpsert` |
| Provider-selected retry lower bound | `JobFailure::retry_not_before_delay` / `retry_not_before` |
| Another successful bounded slice | `JobCompletion::continue_now` / `continue_after` |
| One active workflow per application key | `active_key` + `enqueue_or_get_active_workflow` |
| One job at a time per external resource | `enqueue_job_with_execution_resource` or step `execution_resource` |
| Recover a canceled or dead-lettered direct job | `compare_and_requeue_job` |
| Repeat a successful direct job | `compare_and_replay_succeeded_job` |
| Recover a terminal workflow | `recover_workflow_run` |
| Worker process lifecycle | `Supervisor::run_until_shutdown` |
| Custom worker lifecycle persistence | `JobLeaseIdentity` with `_for_lease` lifecycle APIs introduced in 0.9.0 |
| Admin/status views | `get_*` / `list_*` APIs and `count_workflow_runs` in `runledger_postgres::jobs` |
| Versioned read-only HTTP admin | `runledger_admin::router(AdminService)` mounted by the authenticated host |
| Reusable React admin | `@runledger/admin/client` and `@runledger/admin/react` |

Use `set_job_schedule_active` to pause/resume schedules and
`set_job_schedule_next_fire_at` to retime a schedule cursor.
Use `runledger_postgres::jobs::count_workflow_runs_with_scope` with
`runledger_postgres::jobs::WorkflowRunReadCountFilter` for workflow counters.
Use `WorkflowRunReadScope::Global` for exact global rows,
`Organization(id)` for one tenant, and `Admin` only for trusted all-tenant
surfaces.

For browser-based operator views, mount the state-complete `runledger-admin`
router at `/api/admin/runledger/v1`. The embedding service must authenticate the
caller and insert `AdminAccess`; never derive it directly from an untrusted
request field. `AdminAccess::organization` is exactly tenant-scoped, while
`AdminAccess::all` includes global and every organization's rows. Default to
`DataVisibility::MetadataOnly`; `Full` exposes stored payloads and diagnostic
text. Organization scope also filters workflow steps by their effective
execution organization and hides graph edges unless both endpoints are visible.
Definitions are service-wide and require either `AdminAccess::all` or an explicit
`with_service_wide_definitions()` grant. The v1 router has no mutation actions.
The React package discovers these resources from `/capabilities`, uses controlled
route values, and has no router, query-cache, or design-system dependency.

For transactional handoff before a job definition exists, record a strictly
idempotent `JobEnqueueIntent` in the application's `READ COMMITTED` transaction.
Concurrent recorders for the same key may wait for the transaction that first
claimed it, so include that wait in caller lock ordering and timeout budgets.
Record the intent before any operation in that transaction that can lock a
`job_queue` row. A job-first recorder can create an inverse lock cycle with
retention's canonical intent-before-job order.
A record outcome reports point-in-time lifecycle state, not a promotion
guarantee; an existing intent can be promoted or become conflicted concurrently,
including before a caller-owned transaction ends.
A standard worker later promotes registered, enabled types through the ordinary
enqueue path. Full promotion batches drain immediately; partial and empty
passes wait for the configured cadence. Use `IntentPromoterConfig` for
independent controls. Every worker-enabled supervisor promotes by default and
polls independently when idle. An idle pass is one non-locking eligibility
query, so capacity plans must include that query rate.
Disable only redundant or unused promoters, and retain coverage for every type
that can receive intents. Database failures defer only the affected intent with
bounded jittered backoff and retry indefinitely; inspect promotion attempt/error
metadata and monitor pending age and `conflicted_24h`. Full conflicted evidence
remains available through intent reads/lists. Treat intent payloads and keys as
sensitive queue data and do not log them. Queue retention must call
`delete_promoted_job_enqueue_intents_for_jobs_tx` for its exact selected job IDs
before deleting those jobs in the same transaction. The helper fences
promotion, deletes promoted-intent links, then locks the selected jobs in the
canonical intent-before-job order. The retention transaction must use
`READ COMMITTED`; stronger isolation returns
`job.intent_retention_unsupported_isolation` before fence acquisition. The
helper preserves stricter caller timeouts and
allows up to thirty seconds to acquire the
exclusive promotion fence, then caps each job- or intent-row lock wait at five
seconds; every statement is capped at thirty-five seconds. Timeout and deadlock
errors abort the transaction, which must be rolled back and retried in full.
Deploy that retention path to every queue-retention caller before enabling
intent writers.

## Workflow DAG Rule

If work has step dependencies, build a workflow DAG:

```rust
let run = WorkflowDagBuilder::new("workflow.example", &metadata)
    .job("a", "jobs.a", &payload_a)?
    .job("b", "jobs.b", &payload_b)?
    .after_success("b", ["a"])?
    .build()?;

enqueue_workflow_run(&pool, &run).await?;
```

For workflows that should return a durable JSON result, declare one DAG step as
the result step with `.result_step(...)` or `.try_result_step_key(...)`,
enqueue with `enqueue_workflow_run_handle`, and wait/read through
`WorkflowRunHandle::get_status`, `get_run`, or `get_result`. Handler success
returns `JobCompletion`; use `JobCompletion::with_output(...)` for compact result
metadata. Prefer explicit wait timeouts in production. The default waits up to
five minutes. `timeout: None` opts into unbounded waits and may hold a
PostgreSQL listener connection. Result error codes include
`workflow.handle_storage_error`, `workflow.run_not_found`,
`workflow.result_not_declared`, `workflow.result_missing`,
`workflow.result_unsuccessful_terminal`, and `workflow.result_wait_timeout`.
External step output is valid only with successful external completion; failed or
canceled external completions must not provide output. Retrying completion for a
terminal external step requires matching terminal status and completion metadata;
changed metadata returns `workflow.external_step_conflicting_completion_retry`.
For successful completions, changed output returns
`workflow.external_step_conflicting_output_retry`.

Use `WorkflowRunEnqueueBuilder` and `WorkflowStepEnqueueBuilder` for advanced per-step
settings, external steps, or hand-authored dependency specs.

`WorkflowDagBuilder` validates workflow shape, not job registration. `.job(...)`
fails immediately for blank step keys, blank job types, and duplicate step keys.
`.after_success(...)` / `.after_terminal(...)` fail immediately for blank
identifiers or an unknown target step. Missing prerequisites, self-dependencies,
duplicate dependencies, cycles, empty step lists, blank workflow types from
`new(...)`, and blank idempotency keys fail at `.build()` / `.try_build()`.
Use lower-level builders when call sites should pass explicit `StepKey` and
`JobType` values.

Do not manually orchestrate ordinary workflows by polling job status, enqueueing
dependent jobs from parent handlers, encoding dependency state in payload JSON,
or adding app-owned workflow edge tables.
Direct-job recovery rejects workflow-managed jobs with
`job.workflow_requeue_not_supported`; recover the workflow run instead.
Use `update_job_payload_uuid_array_field` only for direct pending jobs; inspect
`JobPayloadUuidArrayFieldUpdate` for `Updated`, `NotFound`, or rejected updates.

## Handler-Selected Retry Timing

Attach `retry_not_before_delay(delay)` or `retry_not_before(timestamp)` only to
a retryable `JobFailure`. The failed attempt still consumes attempt budget and
keeps the same run number. PostgreSQL schedules the later of ordinary policy
backoff and the handler lower bound; exhausted, terminal, and panicked failures
ignore timing. Use `effective_next_run_at` and `retry_timing_source` for the
committed schedule. `retry_delay_ms` remains the policy delay even when the
handler wins, and `requested_retry_not_before` records the resolved request.

Construct `JobFailure` with its constructors because 0.8 made retry timing
private. `retry_after` and `retry_at` are deprecated in favor of names that make
the lower-bound semantics explicit. Low-level persistence callers construct
the non-exhaustive `JobFailureUpdate` with `new` and optional
`with_retry_timing`.

## Bounded Job Continuation

Direct jobs can use continuation immediately; workflow job steps require the
persisted `WorkflowStepEnqueueBuilder::allow_handler_continuation()` opt-in,
which defaults to false and is invalid for external steps. Use
`JobCompletion::continue_now()` or `continue_after(delay)` only after a bounded,
successful, idempotent slice. Version checkpoints, read the committed value
from `JobContext::checkpoint`, enforce an application-owned logical
deadline/run limit, and use nonzero delays for polling. Continuation does not
consume `max_attempts`, cannot carry final output, and keeps workflow
dependencies blocked until final terminal completion. Canary by job type or
tenant and alert on continuation
rate, run depth, dead letters, and continuation persistence failures. The
external-consumer smoke test is the compile-checked continuation example.
It also exercises pool-owned and caller-transaction recovery, caller-transaction
successful replay plus an idempotent pool retry, and continuation metrics
through the packaged crates.
Use `get_job_continuation_metrics` for stable per-job-type signals:
`continued_24h`, `active_continued_count`, and `max_active_run_number`. Its
optional organization filter uses admin aggregation semantics; `None` means all
scopes, not exact global scope. Active metrics mean the current run was created
by continuation; later admin recovery does not remain `active` merely because a
job has older continuation history.

## Active Workflow Keys

Use `WorkflowRunEnqueueBuilder::active_key` only with
`enqueue_or_get_active_workflow`. Handle `Inserted`, `ExistingActive`, and
`ExistingIdempotent` explicitly. Active claims are global or organization
scoped and release only after terminal work is quiescent. Workflow type is not
part of that scope; namespace keys by type unless cross-type coordination is
intentional. Active keys are non-blank and limited to 512 bytes. Deferred
release after cancellation depends on the lease reaper; stopped reaping leaves
the key reserved until it resumes. `ExistingActive` can carry a terminal
canceled run during that interval.
`enqueue_workflow_run_handle` rejects active-key payloads; match the classified
active enqueue outcome first, then call `workflow_run_handle` with its run ID
and scope when a result handle is needed.

## Durable Execution Resources

Use `enqueue_job_with_execution_resource` for direct work or
`WorkflowStepEnqueueBuilder::execution_resource` for job-backed steps.
Reservation is atomic before leasing; resource-blocked work remains pending at
attempt zero and consumes no worker claim slot. Keys must be non-blank and at
most 512 bytes. Resource keys are global across organizations; namespace them
in the application when tenants must not coordinate. They guarantee mutual
exclusion, not global FIFO; type-restricted workers order only their eligible
types. Mixing claim APIs or distinct worker type filters may reorder contenders
without weakening mutual exclusion.
The direct enqueue returns `JobEnqueueOutcome`; for keyed jobs, the resource is
part of the canonical request and cannot change on an idempotent retry.
A requested batch size is only an upper bound; cross-worker resource races can
return a short batch. Resource-head discovery scans a bounded 1,024–16,384-job
window scaled by batch size; a dense same-key prefix can therefore also return
short. Resource inserts use consistent key order to reduce cross-filter
deadlock risk. Exclusivity is lease-scoped: the reaper releases an expired owner
as it transitions the owning job after heartbeat loss, so provider-side effects
must remain fenced or idempotent if a late handler outlives its lease.
Stopped reaping leaves expired claims reserved; cleanup is bounded by the
configured reaper batch limit. Reaped lease transitions commit before
coordination-claim cleanup. Detailed reaper results expose released-claim counts
and cleanup errors; the runtime logs cleanup failures and batch saturation.
Resource-owner heartbeats renew the claim row, and continuation releases it
between slices so the next slice re-contends.
Successful direct-job replay preserves the source execution resource.

## Workflow Recovery

Use `recover_workflow_run` to replay a terminal workflow as a new run with
durable lineage. It reconstructs canonical enqueue plus append history,
preserves active/resource constraints, continuation opt-ins, and resolved
per-step queue settings, and uses each source step's latest persisted payload.
It is idempotent by source run and request key, does not reuse the source's
workflow idempotency key, and rejects missing/unknown canonical shapes or
unsupported mutation kinds. Never reopen terminal source steps in place.
Recovery request keys are non-blank and limited to 512 bytes. Retention cannot
delete only the recovery run while its source remains because that would erase
the request idempotency guard.
Construct the non-exhaustive request with `WorkflowRecoveryRequest::new`; omit
the organization setter only for an exactly global source. `source_step_id` is
optional lineage context. `recover_workflow_run_tx` requires a caller-owned
`READ COMMITTED` transaction and does not commit or roll it back.

## Direct-Job Recovery And Replay

Use `compare_and_requeue_job` for standalone pool-owning recovery and
`compare_and_requeue_job_tx` for recovery composed in a caller-owned
`READ COMMITTED` transaction. Prefer
`CompareAndRequeueJob::from_observed_job` to copy exact scope, terminal status,
and run number. Always handle `Requeued`, `ExpectationMismatch`, `NotFound`, and
`CancellationNotQuiesced`; only `Requeued` mutates the job.

Runledger 0.11 removes `requeue_job`; upgrading requires a deliberate migration:

- legacy `organization_id: None` was an unconstrained lookup and is not
  `JobScope::Global`;
- `ResetProgressAndCheckpoint` matches legacy state-reset behavior;
- legacy missing/invalid-state/cancellation errors become typed no-mutation
  outcomes;
- `SUCCEEDED` uses the separate successful-replay API rather than recovery.

Use `compare_and_replay_succeeded_job` for a standalone successful replay and
`compare_and_replay_succeeded_job_tx` for replay composed in a caller-owned
`READ COMMITTED` transaction. `CompareAndReplaySucceededJob` requires exact
source scope/run expectations, one stable `replay_request_key` per intentional
replay action, and a reason. Inspect `CompareAndReplaySucceededJobOutcome`:
`Replayed.replay.disposition` distinguishes a fresh job from an idempotent
request retry; `ExpectationMismatch` and `NotFound` create nothing. A replay is
a new run-1 direct job. The replay operation leaves the successful source and
output unchanged, and Runledger persists lineage in `job_replays` and the
replay's `ENQUEUED` event.
Retention cannot delete only the replay queue row while its successful source
remains, because that would erase the request's idempotency guard. Source
deletion cascades lineage, and one retention statement may delete both queue
rows together.
Workflow-managed jobs cannot use direct replay.

For durable event consumers, call `list_job_events` and prefer
`JobEventRecord::decoded_payload()` over hand-decoding Runledger-authored JSON.
Rust consumers should not hand-parse `requeue_kind`,
`replayed_from_job_id`, `replayed_from_run_number`, `replay_request_key`, or
their companion replay fields.
Match `DecodedRequeuedEventPayload::HandlerContinuation` and
`DecodedJobEventPayload::SuccessfulReplayEnqueued` for continuation and replay
provenance. The decoded enums and struct variants are non-exhaustive, so use
`..` in struct patterns, retain final wildcard arms, and inspect
`JobEventRecord::payload` as the raw fallback for `Unknown`, `Other`, malformed,
custom, or future payloads.

## 0.7 To 0.8 Rollout Fence

Apply
`202607250001_harden_continuation_metrics_payload_validation` and migrations
through `202607280005_workflow_recoveries`, then deploy 0.8 to every worker,
reaper, admin, API, CLI, and repair writer with the new paths unused. Activate
only after every 0.7 process and old lease has quiesced; if releases are
skipped, quiesce every pre-0.8 process. A PostgreSQL trigger rejects a
resource-constrained lease without its exact durable claim, so 0.7 workers fail
loudly instead of violating mutual exclusion but can repeatedly roll back
affected claim batches. After activation, never start a 0.7 writer until new
writes are disabled, continuation/resource work is drained, canceled lease
fences have quiesced, and all 0.8 writers have stopped. Follow the PostgreSQL 18
activation/rollback queries in `docs/downstream-agent-guide.md`.

Apply `202607190001_job_replays_and_continuation_metrics` before deploying
successful-replay or continuation-metrics callers; it creates `job_replays` and
`job_continuation_metrics_rollup`. Apply
`202607250001_harden_continuation_metrics_payload_validation` for corrected
continuation metrics. Every migration from `202607190001` through
`202608180001` is SQLx-history-only and intentionally does not advance the
custom compatibility fence, so Runledger's filtered older startup and schema
guards can coexist during expand-first rollout. For code rollback, choose one
strategy:

1. Recommended: leave all additive migrations applied and use
   `migrate_after_idempotency_cutover` or
   `ensure_schema_compatible_after_idempotency_cutover`; these Runledger paths
   filter SQLx history to the migrations embedded in the release. Patch startup
   first if the rollback binary calls raw `MIGRATOR.run(...)`.
2. A raw 0.7 `MIGRATOR.run(...)` rejects `202607250001`, the five
   `20260728000*` rows, and `202608180001`. SQLx 0.8 can leave its session
   advisory lock held on that error; close the disposable connection or pool.
   If startup cannot be patched, use the current artifact to revert those seven
   migrations in reverse order. This erases workflow-recovery
   lineage/idempotency, active claims, resource keys/claims, retry audit fields,
   workflow continuation opt-ins, and enqueue-intent audit/idempotency state
   while retaining the underlying workflow/job rows. A rollback to pre-0.7 raw
   code also reverts `202607190001`, deleting relational replay lineage and
   replay-request idempotency while leaving replay-created queue rows and their
   lineage-bearing `ENQUEUED` events. Explicitly accept these losses before
   using either down-migration path.

## Catalog Rule

Use `JobCatalogDefinitionOverrides` for per-job definition differences from
catalog defaults. Overrides win for fields they set; version, attempts, and
timeout must be positive. Catalog schedule sync owns `is_active` on every sync;
use lower-level schedule APIs when admin pause/resume should own active state.
Active schedules require enabled job definitions. Scheduler catch-up materializes
at most one stale fire, then advances the cursor to the first future fire.

## Worker Runtime Rule

Use `Supervisor::run_until_shutdown` for ordinary worker binaries:

```rust
let supervisor = Supervisor::builder_from_env(&pool)?
    .with_registry(registry)
    .build()?;

supervisor
    .run_until_shutdown(shutdown_signal, std::time::Duration::from_secs(30))
    .await?;
```

Use `worker::run_worker_loop`, `scheduler::run_scheduler_loop`, and
`reaper::run_reaper_loop` only for custom runtime orchestration.
If constructing `JobsConfig` directly, validate it; invalid configs can surface
as `RuntimeError::InvalidJobsConfig` or `RuntimeLoopExit::InvalidConfig`.

Custom runtimes should construct one `JobLeaseIdentity` (available since 0.9.0)
from a claimed job's ID, run number, attempt, and worker ID. On 0.11.0 or later,
pass it to `heartbeat_job_for_lease`, `mark_job_running_for_lease` with a
`JobRunningUpdate`, `update_job_ordinary_progress_for_lease` with a
`JobOrdinaryProgressUpdate`, and the appropriate success/failure/continuation
`_for_lease` completion function. Reuse that value for the claim so fields from
different leases cannot be mixed. The older stage-bearing
`update_job_progress_for_lease` remains a deprecated compatibility wrapper.

## Error Handling

For public surfaces, return `QueryError::code()` and
`QueryError::client_message()`. Use `QueryError::internal_message()` only for
trusted diagnostics. `QueryError::kind()` is reserved for the small
compile-checked cross-crate policy set; ordinary application handling should
branch on stable codes.
